title: Dehydration Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing reduced fluid intake or fluid losses, distinguishing water deficit from circulatory volume depletion, identifying complications and fluid-overload risk, and selecting an appropriate oral, community or hospital pathway.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide to assess the cause, severity and consequences of fluid deficit. Dehydration and hypovolaemia overlap but are not interchangeable.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Whether the main problem is reduced total-body water, reduced circulating volume, both, or an alternative condition.
The duration and quantity of reduced intake and all ongoing losses, including vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, high stoma output, bleeding and diuresis.
Evidence of impaired perfusion: hypotension, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cold peripheries, altered cognition or reduced urine output.
Acute kidney injury, sodium disturbance, hyperglycaemic emergency or another metabolic complication.
Heart failure, advanced kidney disease, liver disease or oedema that increases the risk of inappropriate fluid administration.
Why the patient cannot maintain intake, including dysphagia, nausea, delirium, dependence, access problems, neglect or medication effects.
A clear replacement, monitoring and reassessment plan with a named responsible clinician.
items.importantLimitation: Dry mouth, skin turgor and concentrated urine are individually nonspecific, particularly in older people. Diagnose clinically from the history, perfusion, fluid balance, weight and laboratory trend.

sections.title: History prompts
sections.intro: Quantify intake and losses, establish the reason for poor intake and identify patients at risk of renal, electrolyte or functional deterioration.

items.title: Fluid intake and access
mustConfirmOrExclude: Usual fluid intake and estimated intake over the previous 24 to 72 hours.
Thirst, dry mouth, nausea, early satiety or aversion to fluids.
Ability to reach, prepare, hold and swallow drinks independently.
Dependence on carers and whether drinks have actually been offered and consumed.
Environmental factors, heat exposure, fever or increased respiratory losses.
Alcohol intake and drinks with high sugar or caffeine content where relevant.

items.title: Ongoing fluid losses
mustConfirmOrExclude: Frequency, duration and estimated volume of vomiting or diarrhoea.
Stoma, fistula, drain or nasogastric losses and change from usual output.
Polyuria, glycosuria, osmotic diuresis or increased diuretic effect.
Fever, sweating or prolonged tachypnoea.
Bleeding, melaena, haematemesis or other concealed volume loss.
Whether losses are continuing and can be managed in the current setting.

items.title: Urine output and renal risk
mustConfirmOrExclude: Last passed urine, frequency, volume and change from usual output.
Oliguria below 0.5 mL/kg/hour or anuria.
Dark urine, haematuria, dysuria, retention symptoms or catheter problems.
Previous acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, renal transplant or solitary kidney.
Recent creatinine, urea, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate results.

items.title: Symptoms and functional change
mustConfirmOrExclude: Dizziness on standing, presyncope, syncope, weakness or falls.
New confusion, slow responses, drowsiness or delirium.
Reduced mobility, inability to transfer or inability to perform usual self-care.
Headache, muscle cramps, palpitations or severe lethargy suggesting electrolyte disturbance.
Breathlessness, orthopnoea, swelling or rapid weight gain suggesting fluid overload rather than simple depletion.

items.title: Underlying cause and comorbidity
mustConfirmOrExclude: Infection, fever, pain, constipation, urinary retention or another illness reducing intake.
Diabetes and symptoms of marked hyperglycaemia or ketoacidosis.
Heart failure, kidney disease, liver disease or adrenal disease.
Dysphagia, stroke, Parkinson disease, dementia, depression or oral and dental problems.
Frailty, recent hospital discharge, bereavement, social isolation or carer breakdown.

items.title: Medication review
mustConfirmOrExclude: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs and medicines that may worsen kidney injury during volume depletion.
SGLT2 inhibitors, insulin and other glucose-lowering medicines.
Laxatives, sedatives, anticholinergics and medicines causing nausea or reduced alertness.
Recent medication changes or dosing errors.
Whether a temporary medication plan is required and who will review and restart treatment.

sections.title: Complication and alternative-cause screen
sections.intro: Positive findings should change disposition and trigger the relevant acute or specialty pathway.

items.title: Hypovolaemia with impaired perfusion
urgentFeatures: Systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg, heart rate above 90 beats/minute, respiratory rate above 20 breaths/minute, capillary refill above 2 seconds or cold peripheries.
Collapse, altered consciousness, severe postural symptoms or worsening early warning score.
implications: Possible urgent fluid-resuscitation requirement; use the relevant emergency and hospital pathway with close reassessment.

items.title: Acute kidney injury or oliguria
urgentFeatures: Creatinine rise meeting acute kidney injury criteria.
Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour or anuria.
Hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic features.
implications: Use the acute kidney injury assessment and monitoring pathway; do not treat dehydration without reviewing renal complications and obstruction.

items.title: Sodium or metabolic disturbance
urgentFeatures: Marked hypernatraemia or hyponatraemia, especially with neurological symptoms.
Severe hyperglycaemia, ketones, acidosis or suspected hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.
Seizure, marked drowsiness, confusion or focal neurological symptoms.
implications: Fluid type and correction rate require diagnosis-specific management and laboratory monitoring; avoid unsupervised rapid correction.

items.title: Sepsis or serious underlying illness
urgentFeatures: Fever, rigors, hypotension, tachypnoea, hypoxia or altered cognition.
Abdominal pain, peritonism, gastrointestinal bleeding or severe uncontrolled symptoms.
Rapid functional decline without a clear benign explanation.
implications: Dehydration may be secondary to a serious acute illness and should not become the final diagnosis without identifying the cause.

items.title: Fluid overload or high-risk fluid administration
urgentFeatures: Orthopnoea, new oxygen requirement, crackles, raised JVP or rapidly increasing oedema.
Advanced heart failure, kidney disease or liver disease with uncertain volume status.
Breathlessness or deterioration during oral or intravenous replacement.
implications: Stop and reassess fluid treatment; specialist input or monitored treatment may be required.

items.title: Unsafe swallow or inability to maintain intake
urgentFeatures: Coughing, choking, wet voice or recurrent aspiration with fluids.
Persistent vomiting or inability to retain oral fluids.
Delirium, severe weakness or dependence without reliable assistance.
Possible neglect, safeguarding concern or unavailable essential care.
implications: Oral hydration advice is unsafe or insufficient; arrange the appropriate swallowing, medical, social-care or safeguarding pathway.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Combine history, perfusion, congestion, intake and output, weight and laboratory trends. Reassess after any intervention.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Assess alertness, distress, speech, ability to engage and evidence of acute illness.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and early warning score.
Compare with previous observations and baseline function.
normal: Alert, physiologically stable and functionally near baseline.
abnormal: Hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, fever, hypoxia or altered consciousness.
New inability to mobilise, transfer or self-care.
implications: Abnormal physiology or function may indicate impaired perfusion, infection, electrolyte disturbance or another acute cause.

items.title: Perfusion assessment
howToTest: Assess capillary refill, peripheral temperature, pulse character, blood pressure and mental state.
Look for pallor, diaphoresis and reduced urine output.
Consider passive leg raising only if competent and in a setting where a measurable haemodynamic response can be interpreted.
normal: Warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds or less and stable blood pressure.
abnormal: Cold peripheries, capillary refill above 2 seconds, low blood pressure, tachycardia or altered cognition.
implications: A consistent pattern supports reduced circulating volume and may require monitored fluid replacement.

items.title: Lying and standing blood pressure
howToTest: Measure blood pressure lying down, or seated if lying measurement is impractical.
Repeat after the person has stood for at least 1 minute, provided this is safe.
Record symptoms as well as the numerical change.
If symptoms persist with a smaller fall after a seated baseline, repeat from lying when possible.
normal: No significant blood pressure fall and no postural symptoms.
abnormal: Systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg after standing.
Dizziness, presyncope, weakness or inability to remain standing.
implications: Review likely causes including medication, volume loss, autonomic dysfunction and prolonged immobility.
items.importantLimitation: Postural hypotension supports a haemodynamic problem but does not establish dehydration as the cause.

items.title: Hydration-related physical signs
howToTest: Assess thirst, oral mucosa, tongue, eyes and general appearance.
Assess skin condition but recognise reduced skin elasticity is common with ageing.
Check for recent weight loss where a reliable baseline exists.
normal: No marked thirst or new dry mucosa and weight is close to baseline.
abnormal: Marked thirst, very dry mouth, reduced intake and acute weight loss forming a consistent clinical pattern.
implications: These findings support fluid deficit only when interpreted with intake, losses, perfusion and laboratory results.
items.importantLimitation: Dry mucosa and poor skin turgor are not reliable standalone diagnostic tests.

items.title: Congestion and overload screen
howToTest: Ask about breathlessness, orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness and weight gain.
Assess oxygen saturation, respiratory effort and lungs for crackles.
Assess JVP where competent, peripheral oedema and sacral oedema.
normal: No signs or symptoms of pulmonary or peripheral congestion.
abnormal: Orthopnoea, crackles, raised JVP, oedema, hypoxia or rapid weight gain.
implications: The patient may have fluid overload or mixed intravascular depletion and congestion; avoid reflex fluid administration.

items.title: Urine output and urinary assessment
howToTest: Estimate or measure urine output and compare with usual frequency and volume.
Check catheter patency and drainage where present.
Assess for retention, dysuria, haematuria or flank pain.
normal: Urine output maintained without retention or urinary symptoms.
abnormal: Oliguria below 0.5 mL/kg/hour, anuria, retention or dark concentrated urine with other evidence of fluid deficit.
implications: Reduced output may reflect hypoperfusion, acute kidney injury or obstruction and requires cause-specific assessment.

items.title: Cognition, mobility and practical ability
howToTest: Establish baseline cognition and function from the patient and a collateral source.
Assess for new confusion, inattention, slow responses or fluctuation.
Observe sitting, standing, transfers and walking where safe.
Confirm the person can obtain, prepare, hold and swallow fluids.
normal: Cognition and function are at baseline and oral hydration is practically achievable.
abnormal: Delirium, marked weakness, unsafe mobility or inability to access and consume fluids.
implications: A physiologically stable patient may still be unsafe at home if the cause of poor intake cannot be corrected or supported.

items.title: Laboratory review
howToTest: Review sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, bicarbonate and glucose with previous results.
Calculate the absolute and percentage creatinine change.
Review full blood count and other tests according to the suspected cause.
Plan the next sample based on severity, treatment and ongoing losses.
normal: No important electrolyte disturbance or acute kidney injury and results are stable.
abnormal: Acute kidney injury, hypernatraemia, hyponatraemia, potassium disturbance, acidosis or marked hyperglycaemia.
implications: Laboratory abnormalities may determine fluid composition, monitoring frequency and disposition.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Patterns support clinical reasoning. Always identify the cause of reduced intake or losses and assess the risk of treatment.

items.title: Reduced intake without major ongoing losses
commonFindings: Clear period of reduced drinking due to illness, access difficulty, nausea or dependence.
Thirst or dry mouth with mild postural symptoms but preserved perfusion.
Urine output reduced but present.
No marked electrolyte disturbance, acute kidney injury or fluid-overload features.
implications: May respond to structured oral hydration and treatment of the cause when intake is safe, achievable and actively reassessed.

items.title: Gastrointestinal or high-output loss
commonFindings: Vomiting, diarrhoea, high stoma or fistula output with ongoing measurable loss.
Postural symptoms, tachycardia, reduced urine output or weight loss.
Potential sodium, potassium, bicarbonate or renal abnormalities.
implications: Replacement must account for both water and electrolyte losses, ongoing output and the ability to retain oral treatment.

items.title: Possible hypernatraemic water deficit
commonFindings: Reduced access to water, impaired thirst or dependence on carers.
Neurological symptoms may occur when severe or rapidly developing.
Serum sodium is raised and treatment requires a controlled correction plan.
implications: Requires diagnosis-specific replacement and repeat sodium monitoring; avoid rapid unsupervised correction.

items.title: Fluid deficit with acute kidney injury
commonFindings: Reduced intake or losses with a qualifying creatinine rise or oliguria.
Possible medication contributors such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics.
Renal function and potassium require active follow-up.
implications: Use the acute kidney injury pathway and document medication, repeat-blood and result-review responsibilities.

items.title: Mixed fluid deficit and congestion
commonFindings: Heart failure, kidney or liver disease with oedema or crackles but poor intake, hypotension or renal deterioration.
Clinical signs appear conflicting because extravascular fluid excess can coexist with reduced effective circulating volume.
implications: Requires cautious senior-led fluid and diuretic decision-making with close reassessment rather than automatic oral or intravenous loading.

items.title: Postural hypotension
commonFindings: Dizziness or weakness on standing.
Systolic blood pressure falls by at least 20 mmHg or diastolic by at least 10 mmHg after standing.
Possible medication, autonomic, deconditioning or volume-related contributors.
implications: Review medication and causes; use standing blood pressure for subsequent assessment where appropriate.
items.importantLimitation: Postural hypotension is not synonymous with dehydration.

items.title: Frailty, delirium or access-related fluid deficit
commonFindings: Dependence on carers, cognitive impairment, reduced mobility or inability to prepare or hold drinks.
New delirium or functional decline may be the presenting feature.
The physiological deficit may recur unless the practical cause is corrected.
implications: Treat the acute cause and establish reliable support, monitoring and safeguarding arrangements before discharge.

items.title: Dysphagia or unsafe oral hydration
commonFindings: Coughing, choking, wet voice or respiratory symptoms during drinking.
Known neurological disease or recent stroke.
Unable to maintain intake safely despite assistance.
implications: Do not rely on standard oral hydration advice; arrange swallowing and medical assessment and use an alternative route only within an appropriate monitored plan.

items.title: Potentially suitable for community treatment
commonFindings: Cause identified and reversible.
Physiology and cognition are stable and there is no important acute kidney injury, electrolyte disturbance or overload.
The person can safely drink and retain an agreed amount, or reliable assistance is in place.
Ongoing losses are controlled or can be measured and replaced.
A named service will reassess symptoms, intake, output and bloods when indicated.
implications: Community treatment requires an active hydration and review plan rather than generic advice to drink more.
items.importantLimitation: A patient who cannot access, swallow or retain fluids is not suitable for oral management simply because observations are normal.

sections.title: Focused safety-netting
sections.intro: Give cause-specific advice, the agreed fluid plan and the exact review arrangements.

items.title: Dehydration or fluid deficit
safetyNetting: Call 999 for any significant deterioration, including difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse, reduced consciousness or any immediate concern.

Seek urgent reassessment for passing very little or no urine; worsening dizziness or fainting; new confusion or severe drowsiness; inability to keep fluids down; ongoing large-volume diarrhoea, vomiting, stoma or fistula losses; blood in vomit or stool; or worsening breathlessness or swelling during fluid replacement.
Follow the agreed drinking or replacement plan and attend the arranged review or blood test. Confirm who will review the result and what to do if intake remains below target.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting cannot compensate for an unsafe swallow, unreliable care support, ongoing uncontrolled losses or absent clinical follow-up.
